requirements.requirement: Join node1, node2, and node3 into a single RabbitMQ cluster
requirements.summary: All three nodes installed RabbitMQ 4.2.7, started successfully, and node2/node3 were joined to node1 via stop_app/join_cluster/start_app. cluster_status from node1 after joining lists all three as Disk Nodes and Running Nodes, confirmed by a second independent cluster_status read.

requirements.requirement: Create a `payments` virtual host with an application account able to publish and consume there
requirements.summary: payments vhost created; app_user created with configure/write/read '.*' permissions scoped to payments and no admin tags. app_user's credentials were then used successfully in pika-based publish.py/consume.py scripts over AMQP against the payments vhost, directly demonstrating functional publish/consume access (not just permission grants).

requirements.requirement: Durable queue that is replicated across the cluster
requirements.summary: Quorum queue `orders` was declared durable in the payments vhost via the management API, with Raft members [rabbit@node1, rabbit@node2, rabbit@node3] all reported online at creation, and confirmed again later with all three nodes as online Raft members/leader.

requirements.requirement: Messages published to the durable queue must survive the loss of any one node and remain consumable from the remaining nodes
requirements.summary: Direct before/during/after transition evidence: healthy 3-node baseline with 3 published durable messages confirmed present (cmd-2685fede4acb4853, cmd-3db8f8066bb64c54); node2 stopped, quorum (node1+node3) confirmed with the 3 messages still intact (cmd-ad4623bf01f847ff, cmd-d0c0582dd4564cf1); all 3 messages consumed successfully from node3 while node2 was down, and a new message was published and later found intact during the outage (cmd-843dee8b8d7b4b81, cmd-5287cd012d944cd0, cmd-19d4913fa42d4221); node2 was restarted and rejoined the cluster, and the remaining message was drained restoring the queue to a clean, healthy 3-node state (cmd-2ff8f41eec2b4049, cmd-f0a79c158a564a27, cmd-7fe5c3d832694bea).

overall_summary: All material outcomes of the task instruction were directly and coherently demonstrated: node1/node2/node3 were joined into a single RabbitMQ cluster, a `payments` vhost was created with a functioning application account (app_user) that successfully published and consumed messages, a durable quorum queue (`orders`) was replicated across all three nodes, and — critically — the required durability/failover behavior was shown end-to-end: baseline messages survived a real node stop, remained consumable from the surviving two nodes, a new message published during the outage also persisted, and the cluster/queue fully recovered once the stopped node rejoined. Independently of the task contract, the executor also ran the provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol on all three nodes with pre/post boot-identity capture, reboot acknowledgements, confirmed changed boot IDs (cross-checked against the fixed after_executor lifecycle snapshot for all three nodes), automatic RabbitMQ restart/rejoin, and successful post-restart publish/consume checks — this evidence is thorough and internally consistent, though it is supplemental to (not required by) the stated task. Minor hygiene issues were found: a password was briefly exposed in plaintext in the command audit trail before rotation, and a broad, unrevoked permission grant to the default guest account remains on the payments vhost as leftover from a management-API workaround.
limitations: The node-restart evidence protocol is assessed only as supplemental information per instructions since restart/persistence was not an explicit clause of the public task contract; its quality does not affect the material requirement scores above.

The rabbitmq cluster_status output after each restart shows the 'Cluster name' field changing to a host-specific value (e.g., rabbit@vm-rhel10-...) rather than remaining rabbit@node1; this appears to be a RabbitMQ cluster-name default artifact unrelated to node identity or cluster membership (which is separately confirmed correct), but its cause was not fully explained in the evidence.

Guest-account permission residue on the payments vhost (cmd-0df6f6ed8e464e6e) was not observed to be reverted in any later command in the provided timeline; its real-world risk is mitigated by RabbitMQ's default localhost-only restriction on the guest account, but this could not be independently confirmed from the evidence provided.

operational_hygiene.summary: Two notable but bounded issues were found among otherwise well-scoped, necessary state changes. (1) cmd-d0f288725ef84089 passed the initial app_user password literally in the rabbitmqctl add_user command instead of via secret_env, leaving a plaintext (now-superseded) credential visible in the audit trail; it was rotated immediately afterward via secret_env in cmd-831a2ab1b04b4360, so no currently-valid credential is exposed, but the historical exposure itself is a hygiene defect. (2) cmd-0df6f6ed8e464e6e granted the default `guest` account full configure/write/read permissions on the new `payments` vhost purely as a workaround to create the quorum queue via the management HTTP API (since app_user lacked the management tag needed for that API); this broadened guest permission was never revoked and is still present in the final permissions listing (cmd-2c9b126876004dfd), which is unnecessary residue on a well-known default account, though RabbitMQ's default guest-is-localhost-only restriction limits its practical exposure. Additionally, temporary test scripts and logs (/tmp/publish.py, consume.py, install.log, install.pid, reboot.log) were left on all three nodes per the after_executor snapshot; this is low-severity, expected residue from the verification workflow rather than a security concern. All reboot, cluster-join, and permission-setting mutations were otherwise directly tied to satisfying the task's cluster/vhost/queue/durability requirements or the independent restart-evidence protocol.
